toc.title: The context of a safety cue

blocks.p: Your sensory input can take you out of your safety state without you even realizing it. Here I want to talk about active and passive safety cues, how small passive danger cues build up, and the context of a safety cue.

This came from a question one member asked in a group discussion. What it boils down to is: can sensory overload bring you out of your safety state? And in particular, can washing your hands be a safety cue, or a safety anchor?

I've talked a lot about safety cues and safety anchors, the things that bring you to your safety state. In his book Polyvagal Safety, Dr. Porges specifically lays out passive safety cues and active safety cues.

Passive safety cues are things that are neuroceptive of safety, that might trigger a safety state, but that you're not actively doing. They just come in through your senses. Right now I have a candle on with a pleasant smell, something I got at Target. I think it's a Christmas smell, but I still like it a lot. I can't tell what it is, I just like it. I have a little fake plant here that I like. The lighting in my office, the comfortable seating: I take all of these in passively. I'm not consciously thinking about the scent of the candle, but that scent is still affecting me every moment I'm breathing in. It's just there.

You could mindfully, actively notice these things, experience them, and feel the safety they bring up within you. But on their own, they're passive. When I have the right lighting in here, it's just a passive safety cue.

An active safety cue, or safety anchor, is something you actively do. That could be going for a jog, meditation, breathwork, yoga. I might be broadening it beyond what Porges was discussing. The book is a collection of articles, and I forget the name of that one, but he was specifically talking about rituals, in the context of religion, I believe. Things like chanting, if I'm remembering correctly, and yoga, I think, was in there.

I think the concept easily broadens to other things you do to feel a sense of safety or relief. Swimming. Spending time with friends. Maybe just breathing quietly in a corner and mindfully being with the experience of your breath. These are choices you make and things you go and do. In my opinion, all of them are more active safety cues.
This is really important to understand, and I'm glad he covered it, because it broadens my concepts of the Polyvagal Theory.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: This applies to danger cues too, probably more to passive danger cues: the things that take you out of your safety state, down your Polyvagal ladder, into flight, fight, shutdown, maybe even freeze.

Passive cues can build up. They seem to compile, one on top of the other. That could be a collection of safety cues that brings you up your ladder. But what I'm more focused on here is the collection of danger cues that brings you down your ladder and out of your safety state.
These are small insults to your system. They're passive. They're just there in the environment, and you may not have any control over them, though some you probably could.

ul: Sound. The hum of a heater or air conditioning in the background, a refrigerator hum, the sound of traffic. There's a freeway off in the distance from my office. My office is pretty sound dampened, and I still hear that dull hum. When I'm sitting outside in the backyard, I can definitely hear it. Is that enough for me to get up and run away? No. But it definitely affects my system. If that sound were suddenly gone and there was actual quiet while I sat in the backyard, my mindful experience of my safety state would probably be a lot stronger. That's probably why I notice a big impulse within myself to be in quiet. My wife and I really want a cabin in the woods, a place to escape from everybody and everything and all the sounds, and just have actual quiet. You don't get that in the city.

Lighting. At the time, my workplace had bright white fluorescent lights everywhere, which is kind of the standard when you work at a school district, or probably a hospital. White walls, bright white fluorescent lighting, and a little hum from that too. Not something you really focus on or notice, but it does affect your system. Outside my office there was also the sound of students and teachers, an AC and a heater I didn't control, and a train that passed by a few times a day. All these passive things I didn't control, just there, and they absolutely affected my system.

Faces. When you walk through a store, or into work, and you see people with flat affect, people who aren't smiling. Maybe they're not mean, they just have this blunted, flat affect. That's a small passive danger cue. It's not enough to get you to run away, and hopefully not enough to get you to fight, but it affects your system just a teeny tiny bit, a little insult.

blocks.p: That's different from the big insults to your system. Someone coming at you aggressively with an angry face. Going to a job you absolutely hate, where you feel that hatred intensely. Major family issues erupting that you can't ignore. Media you choose to take in that's constantly saturating you in danger cues: be afraid of these people, hate these people. Those are bigger insults. Maybe we could even call some of them active, because on some level you could choose to stop. You could choose to switch your media. So when I say passive danger cues, I'm not really talking about the big ones. I'm focused on those small environmental pieces that come in through your senses, that you probably don't have control over.

Identifying what brings you to safety is so important, especially for future trauma work. If you're going to delve into more difficult stuff, you have to be able to access and stay in your state of safety in order to deal with it: to feel it, to talk about it, and on some level even relive it. You have to be able to stay in your safety state for that to be successful.

blocks.h: The context of a safety cue

blocks.p: So can washing your hands be a safety cue? Yeah, sure. In general, yes. But what I'm more interested in is: what about washing your hands is the safety cue? Because it's not just the action. Maybe it's rubbing your hands together. Maybe it's the water. Maybe it's feeling clean, or the act of cleaning yourself.

There's more going on when you wash your hands. And this goes beyond this one example. Whatever you feel pulled toward, whether it's washing your hands, jogging, working out, drawing, or swimming, it might not be just the action. There may be more going on contextually that you feel this safety pull toward. So notice the entire context.

Take washing your hands. Usually we're in a bathroom, or at a sink somewhere: a kitchen sink, a public bathroom. Typically, when we go to wash our hands, we're alone or closer to being alone, or at least removed from other people and other potential danger cues. It's a smaller environment, with potentially less stimulation and some sense of aloneness. So you might have a chance to breathe. You might have a chance to slow down. You may be out of a context you don't want to be in. Maybe the lighting in that bathroom is a bit dimmer, and that feels better for your system.

If you're at a really loud restaurant, that may be overstimulating. Going to the bathroom to wash your hands could be an opportunity to escape that overstimulating environment to one with less stimulation. So maybe it's not washing your hands. Maybe it's the change in environment.

There may also be something soothing in the place where you wash your hands. The smell of your soap. A decoration on the wall, maybe some wonderful old shiplap that just feels good to look at. A chance to slow down and breathe in a littler, smaller environment. The temperature of the water, which might just feel good. The feel of the water itself might be a safety cue. So it's not just the action of washing your hands. That could be part of it, but a whole bunch of things come into play.

Same with me and swimming. The action of swimming, the physical movement, is absolutely grounding for me. But my backyard also has a ton of green in it, and I like that a lot. It's very soothing. It's relatively quiet. The dogs can get kind of annoying, sure, and there's traffic. But when I go underwater, I don't hear much of anything. That provides a kind of sensory dampening that my system likes. And a beautiful sunny day is a safety cue in and of itself. So is it just the swimming? No. A whole bunch of stuff comes along with it.
Whatever you feel this pull toward that may feel like safety, notice it, and notice what's actually helping you:

ul: What about the context is actually appealing?
What about the context do you find grounding, a safety cue or a safety anchor?
What's passive in that environment that works for you?
What are you actively doing that works for you?

blocks.p: The sunshine when I go outside and swim is a passive safety cue. Going underwater, swimming, kicking off the walls: that's an active safety cue, something I can do. Notice these pieces the next time you're grounding yourself, and really mindfully experience them.

I really want you to do this, because these things can become default compulsions. You could easily picture someone who keeps washing their hands because something about it feels right. I'm not exactly talking about OCD. I'm using compulsion more generally here, although it might have a lot to do with OCD as well.

Things that seem to make us feel better can become compulsions, in a sense, and that's not a safety anchor. That's something different. That's more of a behavioral adaptation. Compulsive hand washing could totally be that: something we compulsively, or even reflexively, engage in because it somehow seems to do something to our state. It helps us regulate enough that the defensive state isn't out of control. It's not exactly relief. It's just less crumminess. Kind of better. A reduction in pain, maybe.
But that's different. That's a behavioral adaptation, not genuinely a safety anchor or a safety cue. So be mindful of that when you feel a pull, or maybe even a compulsion, toward these things.
